overview: These imported Paleo-Inuit outlines cover Newfoundland. This card follows regional Dorset communities and earlier Groswater traditions, rather than a kingdom. They should not be confused with the later Thule ancestors of living Inuit.

periods.title: Earlier traditions and regional change
periods.summary: Earlier Paleo-Inuit traditions, including Groswater, preceded the main Dorset occupation discussed here.

periods.title: Dorset settlements
periods.summary: At Phillip’s Garden, people returned to substantial houses and rich seal-hunting grounds.

periods.title: Later Dorset life
periods.summary: Fleur de Lys quarrying belongs largely to these centuries, extending beyond the later map endpoint.

items.text: At Phillip’s Garden, large quantities of harp-seal bones show the importance of seasonal hunting. The exposed coast put people near migrating animals. Returning to a productive place could tie the year’s food supply to familiar homes and neighbours.

Dorset soapstone lamps burned animal oil for heat and light. This made household fuel less dependent on finding firewood. Cooking vessels and lamps belonged to a wider stone-working tradition, with local choices shaped by available materials.

Excavations changed the apparent size of Phillip’s Garden houses. Features first interpreted as walls proved to be internal platforms. Once those spaces were included, some houses had much larger footprints than their visible central hollows suggested.

These houses could have raised sleeping areas, storage pits and entrances facing the sea. Substantial construction and repeated use have led researchers to suggest that several families sometimes lived and hunted together. That interpretation is particularly associated with this site.

Not every hollow marks a house occupied at the same moment. Researchers combine mapping, excavation and radiocarbon dates to reconstruct settlement. Phillip’s Garden accumulated through centuries of returning, rebuilding and changing activities, rather than one enormous village census.

At Fleur de Lys, unfinished vessel shapes and removal scars remain in the rock. They preserve stages of making soapstone containers, while spoil heaps and discarded tools reveal the labour around them. A quarry wall can be a record of work.

To begin a vessel, workers prepared the rock face, separated a rough shape, extracted it and finished it. Soapstone was relatively easy to carve, but a pot still required planning and careful blows: one bad crack could spoil considerable effort.

Small, roughly made pots provide a possible glimpse of children. John Erwin argues that low extraction scars and unfinished-looking miniatures may represent young learners copying adults. This is a reasoned archaeological interpretation, not proof that every miniature was a toy.

The Phillip’s Garden tool inventory includes scrapers, needles and awls used in working skins, as well as tools for making other equipment. Preparing and repairing clothing was part of the same skilled material world as manufacturing hunting gear.

Beetle remains help reconstruct changes around Phillip’s Garden. Species with different habitat needs reveal shifts in vegetation; researchers concluded that people harvested trees and altered their surroundings more than previously appreciated. Tiny insects supplied evidence the larger artifacts could not.

Limestone conditions at Port au Choix helped preserve organic remains unusually well. This is why bones and other fragile evidence survive alongside stone. Archaeological detail depends partly on what the soil protects, so equally busy communities can leave very different records.

Carved animals and human figures are known from the wider Dorset world, including Labrador. They are important visual evidence, but no securely deciphered Dorset text supplies a translated sentence. Their makers’ spoken words should not be replaced with invented modern Inuit dialogue.

ending.text: Dorset occupation ended in Newfoundland around 800 CE, beyond both map endpoints. Causes remain uncertain: proposed hunting failures are not a demonstrated explanation. Other Arctic regions followed different chronologies, so this cannot date every Paleo-Inuit tradition’s ending.
